claims.heading: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claims.claim: Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting, but the server must send the responses in the order the requests arrived ✅[^rfc9112]
claims.context: - **HTTP/1.1.** One connection carries one response at a time. Pipelining lets a client send several requests without waiting, but the server must send the responses in the order the requests arrived ✅[^rfc9112], so one slow response holds up the rest. RFC 9113 names this application-layer HoL blocking ✅[^rfc9113]. HTTP/1.1 lists HoL blocking as a reason clients open several connections ✅[^rfc9112]; browsers use about six per host ✅[^marx].

claims.heading: ## 2. Context: why HoL blocking matters, and how each version moved it
claims.claim: , so HTTP/2 features that assumed one total order (HPACK, the priority tree) had to be redesigned ✅[^rfc9114]
claims.context: - **HTTP/3.** QUIC provides streams, per-stream flow control, reliability at the stream level and congestion control across the whole connection ✅[^rfc9114]. Because QUIC streams are independent, a stream that is blocked or loses a packet does not stop progress on other streams ✅[^rfc9114]. The price: QUIC guarantees no order across streams ✅[^rfc9000], so HTTP/2 features that assumed one total order (HPACK, the priority tree) had to be redesigned ✅[^rfc9114].

claims.claim: At around 2% packet loss, HTTP/1.1 users are usually better off ✅[^h3explained]
claims.context: **Why HTTP/2 can lose to HTTP/1.1 on a bad network.** HTTP/1.1's six connections are six independent byte streams: a loss stalls one of them. claims.heading: ## 6. Worked example: the numbers
claims.claim: Under HTTP/3 nothing changes (first data at 25, 26, 27 ms), because each QUIC packet is decrypted on its own ✅[^rfc9001]
claims.context: **The TLS record effect (S4).** Same as S1, but HTTP/2's 12 packets form one TLS record of about 14 KB (below the 16 KB maximum). Under HTTP/2, A's first byte now reaches the application at 82 ms instead of 25 ms, because no byte of a record can be used before the whole record is decrypted ✅[^rfc8446]: here the loss delays even data that arrived *before* it. How large real records are depends on the server; many servers start a connection with small records ⚠️ unverified.

claims.heading: ## 7. Header compression: HPACK vs. QPACK
claims.claim: Because QUIC does not order data across streams, a request stream can arrive before the insertion it references ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: - **QPACK in HTTP/3.** Insertions travel on the encoder stream; request streams carry references. Because QUIC does not order data across streams, a request stream can arrive before the insertion it references ✅[^rfc9204]. The field section then names a *Required Insert Count*, the number of insertions needed to decode it; if the decoder has seen fewer, the stream is blocked until they arrive ✅[^rfc9204].

claims.heading: ## 7. Header compression: HPACK vs. QPACK
claims.claim: The encoder should not write an instruction unless there is credit for all of it ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: - *Flow-control deadlock:* a decoder may withhold flow-control credit on a request stream until encoder-stream data arrives, while the encoder-stream data itself waits for credit. The encoder should not write an instruction unless there is credit for all of it ✅[^rfc9204].

claims.heading: ## 7. Header compression: HPACK vs. QPACK
claims.claim: - *Cancelled streams:* when a stream is reset, the decoder sends a Stream Cancellation instruction so the encoder stops counting that stream's references ✅[^rfc9204]
claims.context: - *Cancelled streams:* when a stream is reset, the decoder sends a Stream Cancellation instruction so the encoder stops counting that stream's references ✅[^rfc9204].

claims.heading: ## 11. How much it matters in practice
claims.claim: - **Loss is rare on many networks.** One estimate: about 0.01% on wired networks and rarely above 2% on cellular; loss is also bursty, which makes it hard to predict which streams a loss hits ✅[^marx]
claims.context: - **Loss is rare on many networks.** One estimate: about 0.01% on wired networks and rarely above 2% on cellular; loss is also bursty, which makes it hard to predict which streams a loss hits ✅[^marx]. In R1, 0.01% loss gives HTTP/3 a mean advantage of 0.10 ms.

claims.heading: ## 11. How much it matters in practice
claims.claim: - **A 2022 testbed study (35 replayed websites, Chromium):** parallel scheduling strategies clearly reduced HoL-blocked bytes; SpeedIndex (a score for how quickly the visible page fills in) improved only a little for the median site at low bandwidth, and mainly for larger sites under random loss; at 10 Mbps differences vanished; bursty loss erased the gains ✅[^sander_blog]
claims.context: - **A 2022 testbed study (35 replayed websites, Chromium):** parallel scheduling strategies clearly reduced HoL-blocked bytes; SpeedIndex (a score for how quickly the visible page fills in) improved only a little for the median site at low bandwidth, and mainly for larger sites under random loss; at 10 Mbps differences vanished; bursty loss erased the gains ✅[^sander_blog]. The authors' advice: keep sequential scheduling for typical low-loss, low-RTT, high-bandwidth conditions, and switch carefully to a parallel strategy on lossy, low-bandwidth links ✅[^sander_blog].
